Rushcliffe's population increased by around 7,900 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population reached nearly 120,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Rushcliffe increased by 7.2%, from just over 111,100 in 2011 to around 119,100 in 2021.

The population here increased by a smaller percentage than the overall population of the East Midlands (7.7%), but at a similar rate to the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Rushcliffe was home to around 2.1 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 1.9 in 2011. This area was among the lowest 30% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in Rushcliffe than across the East Midlands

An older Rushcliffe

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Rushcliffe increased by two years, from 42 to 44 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than the East Midlands as a whole in 2021 (41 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 65 to 74 years rose by around 2,700 (an increase of 25.3%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by just over 1,800 (7.4% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 65 and 74 years increased by 1.6 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Rise in private renting

The increase in the percentage of privately-rented homes was greater across the East Midlands (3.8 percentage points) than in Rushcliffe (1.4 percentage points).

In Rushcliffe, the percentage of private renting increased from 13.3% in 2011 to 14.7% in 2021. During the same period, the regional percentage increased from 14.9% to 18.7%.

The rate of social renting in Rushcliffe increased from 8.4% to 8.6%, while the rate of home ownership decreased from 76.7% to 75.7%.

Private renting in Rushcliffe increased by 1.4 percentage points

Health in Rushcliffe

In 2021, 54.0% of Rushcliffe residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 51.4% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 32.9% to 31.9%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Rushcliffe residents describing their health as "very bad" was 0.8% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 3.2% to 2.9%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in Rushcliffe increased by 2.6 percentage points

Unpaid care in Rushcliffe

In 2021, 5.4% of Rushcliffe residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 8.0% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, 1.4% of residents (aged five years and over) reported providing between 20 and 49 hours of unpaid care each week, compared with 1.1% in 2011. The proportion of Rushcliffe residents (aged five years and over) that provided at least 50 hours of weekly unpaid care increased from 2.0% to 2.1%.

This area had the region’s second highest proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care. Across the region, only Gedling, with 5.6%, had a higher proportion.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Rushcliffe decreased by 2.6 percentage points

Religion in Rushcliffe

In 2021, 44.4% of Rushcliffe residents reported having "No religion", making it the most common response in this local authority area (up from 29.6% in 2011). Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the East Midlands, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 27.5% to 40.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 44.1% of people in Rushcliffe described themselves as Christian (down from 58.9%), while 5.6% did not state their religion (down from 7.1% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Rushcliffe residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 105,600 Rushcliffe residents said they were born in England. This represented 88.7% of the local population. The figure has risen from just under 100,000 in 2011, which at the time represented 90.0% of Rushcliffe's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with around 1,800 Rushcliffe residents reporting this country of birth (1.5%). This figure was down from just over 2,000 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.8% of the population of Rushcliffe.

The number of Rushcliffe residents born in India rose from around 1,000 in 2011 (0.9% of the local population) to around 1,400 in 2021 (1.1%).

In 2021, 88.7% of Rushcliffe residents reported their country of birth as England

National identity in Rushcliffe

In 2021, 4.2% of Rushcliffe residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 3.1% in 2011.

In 2021, just under 1 in 50 people (1.8%) identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.7% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Rushcliffe that identified as "British only" increased from 19.6% to 59.4%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across the East Midlands (2.7 percentage points, from 5.8% to 8.5%) than in Rushcliffe (1.1 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Rushcliffe increased by 1.1 percentage points

Family in Rushcliffe

Of Rushcliffe households, 18.8% included a couple but no children in 2021, down from 20.3% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in five households (22.2%) included a couple with dependent children, compared with 22.9% in 2011. The percentage of single family households including a couple living with only non-dependent children remained at 6.0%.

The decrease in the percentage of households including a couple but no children in Rushcliffe (1.5 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the East Midlands (1.3 percentage points, from 19.5% to 18.2%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.9 percentage points, from 17.6% to 16.8%.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Rushcliffe decreased by 1.5 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of Rushcliffe residents aged 16 years and over, 31.7% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 28.7% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in two people (51.5%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 53.8% in 2011. The percentage of adults in Rushcliffe that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 8.3% to 8.5%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership was greater across the East Midlands (3.8 percentage points, from 32.3% to 36.1%) than in Rushcliffe (3.0 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Rushcliffe increased by 3.0 percentage points

Change in employment

Of Rushcliffe residents aged 16 years and over, 56.8% said they were employed (excluding full-time students) in 2021, down from 59.0% in 2011.

In 2021, just under 1 in 50 people (1.8%) said they were unemployed, compared with 2.5% in 2011. The percentage of retired Rushcliffe residents increased from 24.2% to 26.1%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in Rushcliffe (2.3 percentage points) than across the East Midlands (1.0 percentage points, from 56.1% to 55.1%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.8 percentage points, from 56.5% to 55.7%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Rushcliffe decreased by 2.3 percentage points

Rushcliffe stood out from other areas for working hours

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week fell in Rushcliffe, but rose across England.

In Rushcliffe, the percentage that worked 15 hours or less in a week fell from 10.6% in 2011 to 10.2% in 2021, while across England it rose from 9.7% to 10.3%. During the same period, the regional percentage remained at 9.8%.

The percentage of adults in employment who worked 49 hours or more in Rushcliffe fell from 14.6% to 12.2%, while the percentage of adults in employment who worked 31 to 48 hours increased from 55.5% to 58.8%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in Rushcliffe decreased by 0.4 percentage points

Disability in Rushcliffe

In 2021, 5.6% of Rushcliffe residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 6.9% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under 1 in 10 people (9.8%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 9.1% in 2011. The proportion of Rushcliffe residents who were not disabled increased from 84.0% to 84.6%.

This area had the region’s third lowest proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. Across the region, only Rutland (4.9%) and Harborough (5.1%) had a lower proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Rushcliffe decreased by 1.3 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Rushcliffe

In 2021, 5.7% of Rushcliffe residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 4.2% in 2011. The 1.5 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the East Midlands, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 6.5% to 8.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 89.7% of people in Rushcliffe identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 93.1% in 2011), while 2.8% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 1.8% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.4% in 2011 to 0.9% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
